summary: EVPN and PBB-EVPN offer multihoming through Ethernet Segments in Single-Active or All-Active modes. This RFC introduces Virtual Ethernet Segments, extending those capabilities to cases where the attachment to the customer is not a plain physical link.

eli5.summary: A kid can plug into two outlets for backup. This lets a connection that is not a plain wire still get that kind of backup protection.

questions: how to multihome with evpn virtual es
what is a virtual ethernet segment
what is a grouping ethernet a-d route
subtitle: Lets a single VLAN, pseudowire or LSP get the same multihoming protection that EVPN gives to whole physical links.

tldr.problem: EVPN multihoming protects a collection of physical links, but some providers need to protect individual Ethernet Virtual Circuits, pseudowires or LSPs that share one physical port with thousands of others.
tldr.mechanism: A virtual Ethernet Segment (vES) gets its own virtual ESI, so the normal EVPN and PBB-EVPN procedures run per circuit. Port 'colors' and Grouping routes let one BGP withdrawal signal the failure of a whole port.
tldr.outcome: A single failed circuit disturbs only its own service instance, and a failed port can be handled with a single BGP message instead of one per vES.

today: RFC 9784 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025. It is not obsoleted by or updated by any other RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: From Physical Links to Virtual Segments
sections.content:
EVPN (RFC 7432) and PBB-EVPN (RFC 7623) let a customer site connect to several Provider Edge (PE) devices through an Ethernet Segment (ES), a collection of physical links. An ES can run in Single-Active or All-Active redundancy mode.

This RFC extends the ES to cover a set of Ethernet Virtual Circuits (EVCs, such as VLANs), or other entities such as MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) or pseudowires (PWs). The result is a virtual Ethernet Segment (vES). The scope covers PBB-EVPN, EVPN over MPLS and EVPN over IP (RFC 8365), and excludes EVPN over SRv6.
sections.eli5: Normally backup protection is given to a whole road. This RFC lets a single lane on the road get its own backup plan.

sections.title: Where vESes Are Used
sections.content:
In access Ethernet networks, many EVCs are aggregated onto one physical External Network-Network Interface (ENNI), which is the demarcation between the provider's IP/MPLS core and a third-party Ethernet Access Provider. Each vES is represented by its EVC on that ENNI. A typical ENNI can be associated with several thousands of single-homed vESes, several hundreds of Single-Active vESes, and tens or hundreds of All-Active vESes.

In access MPLS networks, a vES can be a set of individual PWs. When the PWs share the same LSP pair (the ingress and egress LSPs between the same endpoints), the vES can be associated with that group of PWs. If PWs cannot be aggregated, for example because one terminates on a third PE, the vES has to be defined on each PW on each PE. For MPLS/IP access, only Single-Active multihoming is covered; All-Active is out of scope.
sections.eli5: One big pipe can carry thousands of separate little streams. Some streams need a spare path, and the spare path has to be set up for each stream on its own.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
Section 3 lists requirements on top of those in RFC 8214, RFC 7432 and RFC 7623. A PE MUST handle single-homed vESes on a single physical port, and MUST support single-homed and Single-Active vESes together on one port. It MAY support All-Active vESes. A multihomed vES can span two or more ENNIs on any two or more PEs.

  • Local switching: a PE MUST switch locally among different vESes of the same service instance on one physical port.
  • EVC types: an EVC can map to one broadcast domain (VLAN-based or VLAN bundle service) or MAY map to several (VLAN-aware bundle).
  • Identity: each vES MUST have its own virtual ESI (vESI).
  • Monitoring: each EVC SHOULD be monitored independently, and a failure of one EVC MUST trigger a DF election for its vES.
  • Blast radius: failure of an EVC for a single-homed or All-Active vES SHALL NOT affect other EVCs or trigger MAC flushing in other I-SIDs. For Single-Active vESes, flushing MUST be limited to one service instance and to the C-MACs of the multihomed device.
  • Fast convergence: there SHOULD be a mechanism like EVPN mass withdraw so a single BGP message handles an ENNI failure.

For DF election, a vES with m EVCs must work across n ENNIs on p PEs in any order, where n >= p >= m >= 2.
sections.eli5: The rules say each lane needs its own name, must be watched on its own, and when one lane breaks the others should keep going without a fuss.

sections.title: The Solution: Reuse EVPN With a vESI
sections.content:
The solutions in RFC 7432 and RFC 7623 are used as is, except that the ESI is assigned to an EVC, or a group of EVCs or LSPs/PWs, instead of a link. That ESI is the vESI. In EVPN, MAC addresses learned behind a vES are advertised with the vESI, and aliasing, mass withdraw and Ethernet A-D routes all use it instead of the ESI.

For PBB-EVPN the main change is B-MAC assignment, with these refinements:

  • One shared B-MAC per PE for all single-homed vESes (SHOULD).
  • One shared B-MAC per PE per physical port for Single-Active vESes (SHOULD), or one for all Single-Active vESes on the PE (MAY).
  • One B-MAC per set of EVCs forming an All-Active vES (SHOULD).
  • A single B-MAC per vES per PE for Single-Active (MAY).
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new system, each lane just gets its own name tag and the old backup system works on it as before.

sections.title: Designated Forwarder Election
sections.content:
Service carving works as in RFC 7432 and RFC 8584, but at the granularity of (vESI, Ethernet Tag), where the tag is an I-SID in PBB-EVPN and a VLAN ID in EVPN. The default procedure is repeated with changes:

  1. A PE that discovers or is configured with a vESI advertises an ES route with the ES-Import Route Target.
  2. It starts a timer (default 3 seconds), which MUST be the same on all PEs of the vES.
  3. On expiry, each PE orders the IP addresses of all PEs of the vES numerically and assigns ordinals from 0. With N PEs, the PE with ordinal i is DF for Ethernet Tag V when (V mod N) = i.
  4. The DF unblocks traffic. For Single-Active vESes it unblocks ingress and egress; for All-Active it unblocks egress multi-destination traffic. Non-DF PEs block correspondingly.

If an EVC fails and no EVCs remain for the vES on that PE, the PE withdraws its ES route, re-triggering DF election. In Single-Active mode the newly elected DF MUST trigger a MAC flush notification when the multihoming device is a bridge. For LSP and PW based vESes, the non-DF PE SHOULD signal PW status 'standby' to the aggregation PE, and a new DF MAY send an LDP MAC withdraw.
sections.eli5: The backup devices take turns by a simple rule based on their numbers, so everyone agrees on who is in charge of each lane without arguing.

sections.title: Handling EVC Failures
sections.content:
Beyond the usual failures, vESes add one more case: the failure of an individual EVC. RFC 7023 is used to monitor EVCs, and RFC 4377 and RFC 6310 are used for LSPs and PWs.

In EVPN, an EVC failure uses the existing mass-withdraw: the PE withdraws the Ethernet A-D per vES route carrying the vESI of the failed EVC, and remote PEs act as in Section 8.2 of RFC 7432.

In PBB-EVPN, updating the physical port's B-MAC with a MAC Mobility extended community would flush C-MACs for every EVC on that port. Instead, the B-MAC/I-SID route from RFC 9541 SHOULD be used, which flushes only the C-MACs of one I-SID for that B-MAC. A failed EVC with several VLANs needs one such route per I-SID. When an EVC has a large number of I-SIDs, it is RECOMMENDED to assign a B-MAC per vES and simply withdraw it on failure.
sections.eli5: If one lane is blocked, only the traffic in that lane is told to reroute. Nobody else on the road gets bothered.

sections.title: Port Failure and Fast Convergence
sections.content:
When a physical port carrying thousands of vESes fails, sending one BGP message per vES is slow. This RFC adds an optional shortcut built on port colors. By default the color is the port's MAC address, signaled in the EVPN Router's MAC Extended Community (RFC 9135), and it MUST be unique.

  • In EVPN, each vES's ES and Ethernet A-D per ES routes carry the color. The PE also advertises a special Grouping Ethernet A-D per ES route, using a Type 3 ESI with the port MAC and a local discriminator of 0xFFFFFF. The ESI label extended community MUST NOT be added to it.
  • In PBB-EVPN, the color rides on each vES B-MAC route, and the PE MAY advertise a Grouping B-MAC route.
  • On port failure the PE withdraws the Grouping route. Receivers look up the vESes for that color and run MAC invalidation or flushing, and the other PEs in the redundancy group start DF election for all affected vESes at once.

For PBB-EVPN, if the port MAC is the B-MAC source address the PE MUST use an EVPN MAC route withdrawal to flush; if a shared PE MAC is used, it MUST re-advertise that route with MAC Mobility. The first method is recommended because it limits flushing the most. The whole fast-convergence optimization is OPTIONAL, and the Grouping withdrawal should be sent ahead of the individual vES withdrawals.
sections.eli5: Instead of telling everyone about each broken lane one by one, you ring one bell that says everything on this road is broken.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: All security considerations of RFC 7432 and RFC 7623 apply directly. The document adds no new ones, because vES route advertisement and processing follow those of physical ESes in those RFCs. IANA has no actions to take.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added that could be abused, so the same safety rules as before still cover it.
